sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: The front matter of WHO's 2011 policy statement on the use of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle-income countries. It includes cataloguing and copyright details, the table of contents and summary material. It ends with declarations of interest, explaining that experts with IGRA research links and the systematic reviewers did not take part in the GRADE evaluation or in forming recommendations.

sections.extract: Use of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle- income countries Policy Statement 2011 WHO Library Cataloguing-in-Publication Data Use of tuberculosis interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in low- and middle-income countries: policy statement. 1.Interferon-gamma. 2.Tuberculosis, Pulmonary - diagnosis. 3.Immunoassay - methods. 4.Reagent kits, diagnostic. 5.Developing countries.

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Describes the background to the IGRA policy statement, noting that about a third of the world's population has latent TB infection and that the tuberculin skin test long was the only detection tool, with known limitations. It explains how IGRAs work and their growing commercial promotion in high-burden settings. It argues that their role needed evaluation in low- and middle-income countries with limited public health resources.

sections.extract: Background Tuberculosis (TB) continues to have a significant health impact worldwide, with one third of the world’s population estimated to be infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, resulting in so-called latent TB infection (LTBI). sections.title: Evidence synthesis

summary.text: Describes the evidence synthesis behind the IGRA policy, following WHO's process of systematic reviews and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies followed by an Expert Group review using the GRADE approach. It sets out how studies were selected, data extracted and quality assessed. It explains how results were pooled, or summarized when fewer than four studies were available.

sections.extract: Evidence synthesis The systematic, structured, evidence-based process for TB diagnostic policy generation developed by WHO-STB was followed: The first step constituted systematic reviews and meta-analysis of available data (published and unpublished) using standard methods appropriate for diagnostic accuracy studies. sections.title: Decision-making during the Expert Group meeting and external review

summary.text: Explains that the Expert Group reviewed the systematic reviews in advance and reached decisions by consensus, with members' concerns recorded in the meeting report. The final policy was approved by WHO's Guidelines Review Committee.

sections.extract: Decision-making during the Expert Group meeting and external review The systematic reviews were made available to the Expert Group for scrutiny before the meeting. The Expert Group meeting was co-chaired by the WHO-STB secretariat and an evidence synthesis expert. Decisions were based on consensus. sections.title: Scope of the policy guidance

summary.text: Defines the scope of the policy guidance as a pragmatic summary of evidence and recommendations on IGRAs in low- and middle-income countries, intended for national TB programme managers and to be read with the Expert Group report.

sections.extract: Scope of the policy guidance This document provides a pragmatic summary of the evidence and recommendations related to the use of IGRAs in low- and middle-income countries and should be read in conjunction with the detailed findings from the Expert Group Meeting Report. This policy guidance should be used to inform the use of IGRAs in low- and middle-income countries. It is intended for National TB Programme

sections.title: Study characteristics

summary.text: Describes the studies included on IGRAs for diagnosing active pulmonary TB in adults in low- and middle-income countries, limited to the two current commercial assays. It explains how sensitivity and specificity were estimated, the latter only among suspects found not to have active TB.

sections.extract: Study characteristics Studies included were those that evaluated the performance of the most recent generation of commercial, RD1 antigen based IGRAs (QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT) [Celestis, Victoria, Australia] and T-SPOT [Oxford Immunotec, Oxford, United Kingdom]) among adult (>15 years) active pulmonary TB suspects or cases in low- and middle-income countries. sections.title: Summary of results

summary.text: Reports that IGRAs had sensitivity of 73–83% and specificity of 49–58% for active TB in low- and middle-income countries, so about one in four culture-confirmed patients could test negative. It also notes industry involvement in some of the studies.

sections.title: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base

summary.text: Describes the strengths and limitations of the evidence on IGRAs for active TB, including substantial heterogeneity and the steps taken to reduce it. It also notes the lack of standard definitions of high-incidence settings and of data on patient outcomes or preferences.

sections.extract: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base Heterogeneity was substantial for the primary outcomes of sensitivity and specificity. Empirical random effects weighting, excluding studies contributing fewer than 10 eligible individuals, and separately synthesizing data for currently manufactured IGRAs were performed in order to minimize heterogeneity. No standard criteria exist for defining high TB incidence

sections.title: Grade evidence profiles and final policy recommendations

summary.text: Presents the Expert Group's conclusion that evidence for IGRAs and the skin test in diagnosing active TB was of low quality. It gives the strong recommendation against using them instead of microbiological diagnosis in low- and middle-income countries, given the harm of false positives.

sections.title: Study characteristics

summary.text: Describes the studies on IGRAs in children found through the literature search, covering evaluations in 18 countries. Only a minority came from low- and middle-income countries, and definitions of TB suspects and controls varied.

sections.extract: Study characteristics The initial search yielded 234 citations. After full-text review of 68 papers evaluating IGRAs in children, 32 were determined to meet eligibility criteria, covering 33 unique evaluations of one or more IGRAs (hereafter referred to as studies) in 18 countries. sections.title: Summary of results

summary.text: Reports that most paediatric IGRA studies came from high-income countries, and that in lower-resource settings IGRAs and the skin test showed very similar accuracy for latent and active TB in children. It notes implementation issues such as blood collection and manufacturer support for many studies, mainly through donated kits.

sections.extract: Summary of results The majority of IGRA studies in children had been performed in high-income countries and extrapolation to low- and middle-income settings with high background TB infection rates was not appropriate. summary.text: Describes limitations of the paediatric evidence, including very different populations, methods and non-standard reference definitions. Sample sizes were often small, and no data were available on patient outcomes or preferences.

sections.extract: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base Studies included assessed very different populations in diverse settings, with the biggest challenge and limitation related to major differences in methodological approaches across studies and non- standardised definitions of reference standards, TB exposure and TB disease. summary.text: Presents the Expert Group's finding that evidence on IGRAs in children was very low quality. It recommends against using them instead of the skin test for latent or active TB in children in low- and middle-income countries, noting harms of blood collection and unaddressed cost and acceptability.

summary.text: A section heading for the use of IGRAs to diagnose latent TB in people living with HIV.

sections.extract: Use of IGRAs for the diagnosis of LTBI in HIV-infected individuals

sections.title: Study characteristics

summary.text: Describes the studies on IGRAs in immunocompromised people, most from low- and middle-income countries, with wide variation in design and in whether participants with HIV were symptomatic.

sections.extract: Study characteristics The initial search yielded 791 citations. After full-text review of 129 papers evaluating IGRAs in immunocompromised individuals, 29 were determined to meet eligibility criteria, covering 37 unique evaluations (hereafter referred to as studies). Of these, 22 studies were conducted in low- and middle-income countries. There was a high degree of variation in study design and study populations.

sections.title: Summary of results

summary.text: Reports that the best test for identifying people with HIV who could benefit from isoniazid preventive therapy remains unclear, and that IGRAs and the skin test performed similarly in people with HIV. It notes industry involvement in some studies.

sections.title: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base

summary.text: Notes the main limitation of the evidence for people with HIV: no adequate reference standard for latent TB, together with small studies and few head-to-head comparisons.

sections.extract: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base The major limitation was the lack of an adequate reference standard to evaluate the accuracy of IGRAs for diagnosis of LTBI. sections.title: Study characteristics

summary.text: Describes the studies on IGRAs for screening health care workers, very few of them from low- and middle-income settings, with widely varying designs and exposure risks.

sections.extract: Study characteristics The initial search yielded 546 citations. After full-text review of 56 papers evaluating commercial IGRAs in health care workers (HCWs), 48 were deemed to have met the eligibility criteria. Of these, only five (12%) were done in low- and middle-income settings. Studies varied greatly in design, execution, and reported outcomes. sections.title: Summary of results

summary.text: Reports that latent TB prevalence among health care workers depended on the test used and the TB incidence setting, with high skin test positivity and slightly lower IGRA positivity. There was no evidence that IGRAs detected new infections better than the skin test.

sections.extract: Summary of results Results indicated that in low- and middle-income countries:  Prevalence of LTBI in HCWs depended on the test used and the particular TB incidence setting. summary.text: Describes the strengths and limitations of the review on health care worker screening, noting a broad search but only two relevant studies and very limited serial testing and predictive data.

sections.extract: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base The systematic review used a comprehensive search strategy using multiple sources and databases to retrieve relevant studies, including unpublished studies and conference proceedings. sections.title: Study characteristics

summary.text: Describes the studies on IGRAs in contact screening and outbreak investigations in low- and middle-income countries after excluding high-income and in-house assay studies. Most were small and few reported blinding of test interpretation.

sections.extract: Study characteristics The initial search yielded 608 citations. After full-text review of 99 papers evaluating commercial IGRAs in screening of contacts and outbreak investigations, 65 studies conducted in high-income countries were excluded, as were 18 studies using pre-commercial and in-house IGRAs. 16 studies were deemed to have met the eligibility criteria. sections.title: Summary of results

summary.text: Reports widely varying rates of positive skin tests and IGRAs among contacts across studies and groups, with generally comparable detection of latent TB. It notes manufacturer support for some studies, including kit donations.

sections.extract: Summary of results Results indicated that in low- and middle-income countries:  The prevalence of positive tests varied greatly between studies and across assays. Prevalence of positive TST results ranged from 22% in children less than 5yrs to 84% in adult HCWs exposed to a smear-positive TB case. sections.title: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base

summary.text: Explains that data on contact screening could not be pooled because of heterogeneity, and that most studies were cross-sectional with inconsistent exposure categories.

sections.extract: Strengths and limitations of the evidence base Due to significant heterogeneity in study designs and outcomes assessed in each study, it was not appropriate to pool the data. After full-text review of 14 papers evaluating the predictive value of commercial IGRAs for active TB, 8 studies conducted in high-income countries were excluded, as were three studies using in-house IGRAs. summary.text: Reports that over 95% of people with positive IGRAs did not develop active TB during follow-up. IGRAs and the skin test performed comparably in predicting disease.

summary.text: Presents the strong recommendation that neither IGRAs nor the skin test be used in low- and middle-income settings to predict which individuals will develop active TB.

sections.title: Operational aspects on the use of IGRAs

summary.text: Summarizes the limited evidence on operational aspects of IGRAs, such as high cost, reproducibility and indeterminate results, and their need for well-equipped laboratories and trained staff. It contrasts these with the skin test's practical limitations.

sections.extract: Operational aspects on the use of IGRAs Only a few studies addressed these aspects, mainly in the discussion and not systematically:  Cost Cost of IGRAs was mentioned by four studies, stating that the assays are too expensive and therefore a limitation to their use.  Reproducibility Only one study addressed reproducibility of T-SPOT by assessing inter-observer agreement, showing excellent correlation. sections.title: Overall conclusions

summary.text: Sets out the overall conclusions that evidence on IGRAs in low- and middle-income countries is limited and of low quality, neither test predicts progression or diagnoses active TB, and replacing the skin test with costlier IGRAs is not recommended.

sections.title: Implications for further research

summary.text: Calls for well-designed research on more accurate IGRAs, including representative populations, prospective follow-up, blinding and evaluation of patient impact.

sections.extract: Implications for further research Targeted further research to identify IGRAs with improved accuracy is strongly encouraged. Such research should be based on adequate study design and including quality principles such as representative suspect populations, prospective follow-up and adequate, explicit blinding.
